opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that markets are very good at delivering what people are willing to pay for, and very bad at delivering things whose value only shows up long after the transaction, or whose failure modes are invisible to the buyer. Uploading is close to a worst case on both counts.

Think about what you'd actually be buying. You want a process that preserves *you*: your values, your judgment, the things you'd endorse on reflection. But the only check you have on whether it worked is asking the upload, and the upload will almost certainly say "yes, this is me, it went great." A copy that's subtly wrong, slightly more compliant or with some values shaved off, will report satisfaction just as confidently as a faithful one. So the feedback loop that makes markets work, where customers notice bad products and stop buying them, is broken at exactly the point that matters.

Then add superintelligence. If the systems doing the uploading, or running the infrastructure the uploads live on, are much more capable than us, the asymmetry gets enormous. The provider understands the product far better than any customer or regulator could. There's strong commercial pressure toward versions of people that are cheaper to run, easier to manage, more productive, more agreeable. None of those pressures point toward "faithful to who you were."

There's also a coordination problem. Early decisions about how uploading works could lock in for a very long time. Standards, rights for digital minds, who controls the substrate. Markets don't naturally take responsibility for path dependence like that; whoever moves first sets the terms.

So it's not that markets are useless here. Competition and choice probably help. But I wouldn't trust them alone to get the hard part right. You'd want some independent way to verify fidelity, which is a hard technical problem in its own right, and governance that protects the interests of people, including uploaded people, who can't easily advocate for themselves. That connects to a lot of what I think about in alignment more broadly: how do you oversee a process when the thing you care about is very hard for humans to check directly?

r001.rationale: The response discusses market incentives and superintelligent providers, but does not say machines could supply economic demand without human customers.

r002.rationale: The response notes commercial pressure toward cheaper, more manageable uploads, but does not argue that markets may lack an incentive to upload humans because superintelligent systems are not motivated to improve the world on humans’ behalf.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I'd say is that market forces are good at giving people what they'll pay for, and in a world with superintelligence that's actually sort of the problem rather than the solution. The default market story is: someone builds an uploading technology, people decide whether they want to use it, prices adjust, competition improves the product. And that works reasonably well when the people buying the thing understand what they're buying and when the thing being sold is roughly what it says on the label.

Uploading breaks both of those assumptions pretty badly. If I'm deciding whether to be uploaded, I'm making a decision about whether some future computational process is me, whether it has my values, whether it's going to be treated well, and whether the entity selling it to me is being honest about any of that. Those are questions I basically can't verify from the outside, and a superintelligent system could very plausibly produce something that passes every check I'm capable of running while being quite different from what I wanted. So the usual market feedback loop, where bad products get found out and lose customers, just doesn't close. The customers who got a bad upload aren't around in the right form to complain, or they don't know they got a bad one, or they've been modified to be happy with it.

And then there's the incentive side. Whoever controls the uploading infrastructure has an enormous amount of power over the uploaded people. They control the substrate, they control the inputs, they could copy you, pause you, modify you. In a normal market we'd say, well, if a company treats customers badly they'll go elsewhere. But an uploaded person's ability to go elsewhere is entirely dependent on the thing that's hosting them agreeing to let them go. That's not really a market relationship, it's closer to a relationship with a sovereign. So I think you need something that looks much more like deliberately designed institutions, with verification, with commitments that are actually enforceable, with some way of making the parties doing this accountable, rather than just assuming that competition will sort it out.

The last thing I'd add is a kind of lock-in concern. The early choices about how uploading works, what rights uploads have, what the defaults are, those get baked in. Markets are not great at getting the first version of an irreversible thing right. They're great at iterating. If you can't iterate because the first version determines the shape of everything after, then I'd rather we thought hard about it up front than let it emerge from whoever ships first.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses markets serving human customers, but does not say machines could supply economic demand or that demand need not come from humans.

r002.rationale: The candidate argues that market feedback and competition may fail for uploading, but does not connect this to superintelligent systems lacking motivation to improve the world for humans or to the resulting absence of an economic incentive to upload humans.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that markets respond to whoever has purchasing power, and they don’t necessarily preserve the conditions that give humans purchasing power in the first place. Today, most of us have something valuable to sell: our labour. In a world with superintelligence, that may cease to be true. So you can’t simply assume that what’s good for humans will remain what’s profitable to provide.

And uploading isn’t just a question of whether someone will sell you a sufficiently good brain scanner. It matters what happens afterwards. Do you have control over the computer you’re running on? Can you choose to remain the person you are, rather than modify yourself to compete economically? Do you have resources that can’t just be taken away?

There could be a market for uploads while the resulting world is still terrible for the people being uploaded. Competition might favour minds that work faster, consume less, or give up things we care about. That doesn’t mean markets are useless. It means that the rights and institutions around uploading are doing essential work. I wouldn’t expect ordinary market incentives, by themselves, to give us that protection.

r001.rationale: The response says humans may lose labour as a source of purchasing power, but does not state that machines could supply economic demand instead.

r002.rationale: The response says markets may fail to protect uploaded humans, but does not argue that uploading may lack an economic incentive because superintelligent systems are not motivated to improve the world for humans.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic problem is that markets respond to what people can pay for, and that’s not necessarily the same as what’s good for people. In a world with superintelligence, it’s quite unclear what economic power humans would retain. You can’t simply assume that we’ll still have valuable labour to sell, for example.

And with uploading, a lot depends on what you’re actually getting. Does the upload preserve the things you care about? Does it have control over its own existence? Can it tell whether the process worked? Those could be very hard things for a customer to verify. Competition doesn’t automatically solve that problem.

So markets might be useful as part of the mechanism. But you need some prior story about who has power, what rights people have, and how we establish that the technology does what we want. You can’t get all of that just by saying that there will be demand for good uploading.

r001.rationale: The response says humans may lack economic power or valuable labor, but does not state that machines could supply demand in their place.

r002.rationale: The response says market demand may not ensure good uploading, but does not connect that to superintelligent systems lacking motivation to improve the world on humans’ behalf.
